idiom_name: getter plus private cache slot invalidated by setters
implementation_notes: A getter over a private field is the local idiom: the cache slot (null or undefined = dirty) is rebuilt on read, and every setter (or a single invalidate()) empties it. Private class fields keep both the cache and the primary state out of the public surface, so the invariant has one home; JavaScript's dynamic nature means nothing else enforces it, since mutating a nested object or array never goes through the setter. The classic full structure is justified when the computation is expensive and the source changes far more often than the value is read; for one-off or trivially cheap values, computing in the getter every time is simpler. In UI code the same effect is usually delegated to a reactive library (see the reactive-computed variant).
pitfalls: One mutator that forgets to empty the cache (or a mutation through a contained object) serves stale data; only a single choke point or a Proxy trap keeps the invariant.
`??=` only invalidates for null/undefined while `||=` also recomputes for 0, '', false - and neither can distinguish a legitimately cached null from 'not computed'.
Private fields are not accessible to subclasses or the outside world: tests and mocks must go through the accessor, and monkey-patching a private state is impossible by design.
Because the getter is a plain function, it is invisible to frameworks that track dependencies; do not expect a re-render to follow a cache rebuild unless the cache feeds reactive state.

variants.name: Proxy set trap that invalidates automatically
variants.idiom_name: Proxy with a set/deleteProperty trap marking the cache dirty
variants.implementation_notes: A Proxy can own the invalidation: the set (and deleteProperty) trap marks the cache dirty whenever any property of the target is written, so call sites cannot forget to mark and the recording is structural rather than conventional. The cost is indirection and identity - the proxy is a different object from the target, property access is slower, private fields are not forwarded, and every method that runs against the proxy must handle `this` being the proxy. For plain state objects this replaces the explicit setter; for hot data structures and classes with private state it is usually the wrong trade.
pitfalls: A trap must not violate Proxy invariants (non-configurable, non-writable properties) or the runtime throws a TypeError when the target is written.
Proxy identity is not target identity (`proxy !== target`) and private fields are not forwarded, so a method called on the target bypasses all traps.
Re-entering the trap through Reflect with the wrong receiver recurses infinitely; always forward with the receiver the trap was given.
Auto-invalidation marks on every write, including writes that do not affect the derived value, so a coarse Proxy can invalidate far more than the explicit setter would.

variants.name: Reactive computed value (framework-managed dirty flag)
variants.idiom_name: Vue computed() / MobX computed over observable state
variants.implementation_notes: In UI code the pattern is normally not written by hand: Vue's computed() and MobX's computed track the reactive dependencies of a getter, cache its result and re-evaluate it only when one of those dependencies changed - the dirty flag, the invalidation edges and the recomputation timing are all framework state. Vue documents the caching explicitly (a computed re-evaluates only when a reactive dependency changes; a method call would run every render), and MobX documents the laziness (values suspend entirely while nothing observes them). Reach for hand-written flags outside the reactive graph - workers, plain data structures, libraries - and beware the framework-specific semantics: dependency precision, suspension, and keepAlive-style options all change when the recomputation actually happens.
pitfalls: Computed values suspend when nothing observes them (MobX) or depend on reactive context: reading outside a reaction may recompute every time, and keepAlive/workarounds risk memory leaks.
Only reads of tracked properties count as dependencies; reading untracked state (Date.now(), a plain object) produces a value that never invalidates.
Writes inside a computed getter (or rebuilding an observable in place) violate the framework's rules and either warn or loop.
A framework computed is not a general-purpose cache: it lives for the component/reaction lifetime, not for the object, and keying it by arguments needs a different structure.
